- Why most likely: Clinical picture of hundreds of small, progressively erupting papules over years fits eruptive melanocytic nevi. Biopsy shows circumscribed melanocytic nests at tips of rete ridges, lack of confluent junctional growth, no mitoses, and normal Ki‑67 — all features favoring benign/indolent melanocytic nevi despite moderate cytologic atypia. Distribution on palms/face/trunk can occur with numerous nevi.

2) Eruptive spitzoid melanocytic proliferations (disseminated Spitz-type nevi)
- Why possible: Histology with pigmented epithelioid melanocytic nests and moderate cytologic atypia is compatible with spitzoid morphology. Low proliferation and absence of mitoses favor benign spitzoid nevi rather than spitzoid melanoma. Disseminated/eruptive spitzoid nevi are rare but reported.

3) Atypical (dysplastic) nevus syndrome with widespread nevi
- Why considered: Moderate cytologic atypia on biopsy raises possibility of many dysplastic nevi. Clinical multiplicity and progressive appearance could reflect an acquired predisposition to numerous atypical nevi even without family history.

4) Cutaneous metastatic melanoma with diffuse pigmented deposits
- Why less likely but must be considered: The diffuse dark papules and mucosal/scleral involvement can be seen with metastatic melanoma or diffuse melanosis secondary to melanoma. Biopsy findings (no mitoses, normal Ki‑67, lack of confluent junctional growth) argue strongly against this, so this is lower probability.

- Why unlikely but included: Mucosal and scleral pigmentation might suggest mucocutaneous lentiginosis. However, the presence of true melanocytic nests on histology (rather than simple lentiginous hyperpigmentation) makes this less likely.

- Full skin examination with total-body photography/dermoscopic mapping and regular surveillance photography to document new lesions and detect changes.
- Targeted excision of any lesions that are larger, evolving, ulcerated, symptomatic, or histologically ambiguous for complete histologic assessment.
